title: Inference instance econ grid exploration
content:
Purpose:
This spreadsheet-style working doc explores a compact sensitivity grid that maps GPU instance families (NVIDIA A10 / L4 / A100 / H100) to operational cost metrics ($/token), energy efficiency (tokens/W), and recommendation heuristics for typical inference workload archetypes (short-chat, long-form generation, embedding-only, reranking). The goal is a pragmatic decision matrix teams can use to pick instance classes and config knobs (batch size, quantization, KV cache hit rate) for predictable unit economics.

Summary Findings (short):
- L4 is most cost-effective for short-chat and dense embedding workloads at small batch sizes when 8-bit quantization is acceptable.
- A100 gives best tokens/W for long-form autoregressive workloads at medium/large batch sizes, but $/token can flip if tail-latency SLOs force low batching.
- H100 shows an advantage only for very large sequence length + model sizes (70B+) or heavy mixed-precision kernels; otherwise premium cost reduces value.
- A10 is a good entry-level instance when throughput requirements are modest and cost-per-hour is constrained; good for staging, low-QPS producers.

Assumptions and core formulas used in the sheet tabs (text):
- Instance hourly price values are cloud list prices (on-demand) normalized to USD.
- Worker efficiency metric: tokens_per_second measured from micro-benchmark; tokens/W = tokens_per_second / GPU_power_draw_watts.
- Amortized $/token = (instance_hourly_price / seconds_per_hour) / tokens_per_second = instance_hourly_price / (3600 * tokens_per_second).
- Effective $/token with KV caching: $/token_effective = $/token * (1 - cache_hit_rate) + cost_cache_miss_overhead (approx modeled as additional 0.15 * $/token for external combiners).
- Quantization delta modeled as: tokens_per_second_quant = tokens_per_second_float32 * speedup_factor[q], where q in {fp32:1.0, fp16:1.1, int8:1.25, awq:1.35}.

Notes on interpretation and sensitivity knobs:
- Cache hit rate is a lever with high impact: moving from 0.1 -> 0.5 cache hit reduces effective $/token by ~30-45% depending on baseline tokens/s.
- Batch size increases tokens/s superlinearly up to kernel saturation; we model diminishing returns past a benchmarked saturation point (see microbench tab).
- For tail-latency sensitive endpoints (p95 < 150ms), prefer L4 or A10 with smaller batch sizes; for batch background jobs choose A100.

Quick recommendation matrix (short text bullets):
- Fast interactive chat (strict p95 <150ms, <100 tokens): L4 int8 or A10 fp16 depending on budget; set batch cap=8, enable KV cache, prioritize throughput per watt.
- Low-cost embeddings fleet: L4 with medium batch sizes (16-32) or A10 for minimal infra spend; aggressively shard and use int8/awq.
- Long-form generation at scale: A100 (or H100 if model sizes exceed 70B or special kernels) with large batch windows and fp16 or int8 with accuracy validation.
- Reranking: use embeddings on L4 for generation of candidate vectors, if scoring is heavy use mixed-instance pool with A100 for heavy scoring bursts.

Appendix: microbenchnotes and TODOs (working):
- Need to run full power-draw sweeps for A100/L4 across seq_len 64/512/1024 and batch sizes 1/4/16/64 to calibrate tokens_per_watt.
- Validate AWQ quantization speedups on our 30B/70B family models (open-source variants).
- Build automated script to convert bench CSVs to this sensitivity grid for continuous benchmarking.
- Action: Marcus to add spot pricing scenario and reserved instance amortization sheet.

Raw formulas used (for reviewer reproduction):
- tokens_per_second = measured_samples_tokens / wall_time_seconds
- tokens_per_watt = tokens_per_second / avg_power_watts
- $/token_raw = instance_price_hr / (3600 * tokens_per_second)
- $/token_effective = $/token_raw * (1 - kv_cache_hit_rate) + ($/token_raw * cache_miss_overhead_factor)
